newsitem.title: UK: UK government loses vote after "cheating" charge.
newsitem.headline: UK government loses vote after "cheating" charge.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives has lost a vote in parliament after opposition parties said they would stop cooperating with the government, accusing of "cheating" in an earlier vote.
In a Tuesday vote on a Labour Party amendment to a bill on stalking -- the practice of harassing victims by following them around -- the government was defeated by 179 votes to 172.
Although there was no immediate threat to the government's survival, the result underlined the difficulties Prime Minister John Major's party now faces in parliament.

The decision by the opposition to withdraw cooperation has hurt Major's hopes of hanging on to power after he lost his overall majority in the lower House of Commons following a by-election last week.

The threat by the opposition Labour party and the minority Liberal Democrats heralds parliamentary trench warfare in the New Year, which will make it harder for Major to push through legislation and hang on until the latest election date in May.

The two parties said they had decided on the drastic step after discovering "double counting" in Monday night's key vote on European fishing policy. The government won the vote, ensuring its continued survival.

"Prima facie, this is cheating and it's never happened before," said Archie Kirkwood, Liberal Democrat business manager. He said he expected most other smaller opposition parties in parliament to follow suit.
Monday's vote was Major's first test of government unity since Labour's by-election victory last week left it tied at 323 seats with opposition parties in the House of Commons.
The government offered concessions to fishermen in Northern Ireland in a successful bid to convince a group of Northern Irish Protestant MPs to abstain in the vote.
In the end, Major won by 316 votes to 305.

But Labour Party chief parliamentary manager Donald Dewar said the government had offered both Labour and Liberal Democrats the same three names of MPs for "pairing" -- a system to allow MPs to be absent for key votes without affecting the overall result. This inflated Conservative support.

"The pairing system is based on trust. If trust is destroyed, the system is unworkable...It smacks of deceit and dishonesty. It is doubly offensive when this manoeuvring is promoted...as 'a resounding success' for the government.
"We have in all the circumstances decided...there will be no pairing arrangements from the return of the House (from holiday) in January," Dewar, flanked by Kirkwood, told a news conference.
Their decision means the government can be ambushed at any minute, making life difficult for its MPs who will have to stay long hours in parliament in case a vote is called suddenly.
Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said the opposition's attitude was a "ludicrous overreaction" as the government would have won even if the pairing had been perfect.

"We have to live together and what I know is that this will damage British interests. It will make it impossible for ministers to go abroad ... I have never heard such hysterical nonsense in all my life," said Heseltine.
The Conservatives are keen to stay in power as long as possible to allow tax cuts which take effect in April to filter through into voters' pockets.
But Labour wants to force an early vote to capitalise on its huge opinion poll lead, currently at 20 points or more.
